summary: Describes open research challenges for network virtualization, comparing its path to how cloud computing moved applications and storage onto remote virtual resources. It looks at moving network functions the same way. It is informational and comes from a research group.

plainLanguage.summary: Cloud computing let people rent computers instead of owning them. This document asks what is hard about doing the same for the network itself.

questions: what are open problems in network virtualization
what are the challenges in moving network functions to the cloud
how is network virtualization different from cloud computing
subtitle: Open problems in network virtualization for research and standards

tldr.problem: Network virtualization aims to move networking functions from dedicated physical hardware to virtualized, shared compute resources, following the cloud computing model. However, many research and engineering challenges exist in quality of service, performance, multi-domain systems, network slicing, service composition, and security.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys open challenges in network virtualization across virtualization technologies, QoS guarantees, energy efficiency, 5G network slicing, service composition, device virtualization, security, control separation, function placement, and testing methodology.
tldr.outcome: The document identifies gaps where new IETF and IRTF standards and research work are needed to make network virtualization practical for service providers and edge computing scenarios.

today: RFC 8568 is Informational and represents the consensus of the NFVRG. It has not been obsoleted. The challenges it identifies remain active areas of research and standards development in network virtualization, edge computing, and 5G deployment.

sections.title: Network Virtualization and Cloud Computing Parallels
sections.content:
Network virtualization takes inspiration from cloud computing: just as cloud computing moved applications and storage from local, dedicated hardware to remote virtual functions accessible through the Internet, network virtualization aims to move networking functions from specialized hardware nodes to a virtualized pool of resources. Network operators are drawn to this approach to reduce costs, improve flexibility, and support dynamic scaling of services across data centers.

However, network virtualization is considered a harder problem than cloud computing because it must virtualize not only computing and storage, but also the network itself. The RFC represents the consensus of the Network Function Virtualization Research Group (NFVRG) and identifies technical challenges that must be addressed in research and standards work.
sections.plainLanguage: Cloud let you rent a computer in the sky instead of buying one. Network virtualization wants to do the same for routers and network boxes.

sections.title: Related Technologies and Frameworks
sections.content:
Network virtualization overlaps with several related domains. Software-Defined Networking (SDN) separates the control plane (which decides how to route packets) from the forwarding plane (which actually sends them), allowing centralized control. Network Function Virtualization (NFV), defined by the ETSI ISG, consolidates many types of network equipment into standard servers and switches running virtualized network functions (VNFs). The NFV management framework (NFV-MANO) includes an orchestrator (NFVO), VNF managers (VNFM), and infrastructure managers (VIM).

Other relevant frameworks include the ITU-T functional architecture for SDN, multi-access edge computing (MEC) for moving services closer to users, IEEE's OmniRAN, and open-source initiatives like OpenStack and OpenDaylight. Service function chaining (SFC) orders service functions through which traffic flows.
sections.plainLanguage: Several groups are working on this: SDN centralizes decisions, NFV virtualizes the equipment, and MEC puts services closer to users. All are related.

sections.title: Quality of Service and Performance
sections.content:
A primary challenge is guaranteeing quality of service (QoS) in virtualized environments. Virtualization introduces overhead; multiple VNFs share underlying compute and network resources, leading to resource contention and unpredictable performance. Solutions include selecting appropriate virtualization technologies (containers vs. hypervisors), developing metrics to characterize VNF performance, using predictive analysis to anticipate resource needs, and ensuring portability of VNFs across infrastructure from different vendors.

Performance improvement challenges include energy efficiency (balancing service availability with power consumption) and improved link utilization. The RFC notes that traditional network performance metrics must be adapted to account for the virtualization layer.
sections.plainLanguage: When many virtual routers share one physical computer, they slow each other down. Figuring out how to predict that and fix it is hard.

sections.title: Architectural and Service Challenges
sections.content:
Deploying network virtualization across multiple administrative domains (multi-tenancy) raises isolation, routing, and interoperability questions. Network slicing for 5G networks requires creating isolated virtual networks on a shared infrastructure, each potentially serving different service types (voice, video, machine-to-machine). The RFC discusses virtual network operators (VNOs) that lease infrastructure and resell slices, and the challenge of extending virtual networks to IoT and edge devices.

Service composition chains multiple VNFs to deliver a service; ordering, placement, and resource allocation across VNFs is complex. Device virtualization addresses whether and how to virtualize end-user devices (e.g., CPE, routers, gateways). Each raises questions about control, management, and user experience.
sections.plainLanguage: One data center might need to run multiple phone networks, each isolated. Connecting them together and to edge devices is complicated.

sections.title: Security, Placement, and Testing
sections.content:
Security and privacy are paramount: VNFs must be isolated from each other, and sensitive operator data must be protected across shared infrastructure. Separation of control concerns requires clear boundaries between management (operation and configuration) and control (routing decisions). Network function placement is an optimization problem: where should VNFs be instantiated to minimize latency, cost, or energy? The solution depends on traffic demands, resource availability, and inter-function dependencies.

Testing of virtualized network functions differs from testing hardware. Methodology must account for variations in underlying infrastructure, the ability to dynamically scale functions, and the need to test new functionality. The RFC calls out the need for new testing frameworks and standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping virtual routers from spying on each other, choosing where to place them, and testing if they work correctly are all unsolved problems.

sections.title: Technology Gaps and Future IETF and IRTF Work
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several areas where the IETF and IRTF could contribute standards and research. These include protocols and mechanisms for VNF lifecycle management, service chaining and orchestration, reliability and failover, energy management, and testing. The NFVRG itself plans to focus on emerging areas such as machine learning for resource placement and management, edge computing, security architecture for virtualized environments, and the integration of network virtualization with 5G and SDN standards.

The document emphasizes that network virtualization is still a maturing field, and the challenges identified are opportunities for research groups and standards bodies to shape how network infrastructure evolves.
sections.plainLanguage: There's lots of work ahead to standardize how virtual networks are built, managed, secured, and tested.
